summary.suggested: The St. Louis Globe-Democrat described fixed or mob-ruled prize fights tied to St. Louis, saying mobs denied Allen his 1869 wins over McCoole and Gallagher and that he faked a broken arm to end his 1870 fight with Mace.

metadata.notes: Masthead: St. Louis Daily Globe-Democrat, Sunday Morning, February 5, 1882, page 6.

facts.fact: Allen came to St. Louis as a stranger, an Englishman sent to Billy Carroll as one willing to fight any man at any time

In the McCoole fight on Foster's Island ($1,000 a side), Allen was winning after nine rounds when Jack Smith hit him in the eye with a stake and McCoole's backers cut the ropes and threatened referee Val McKinney with pistols and knives
The paper said referee Val McKinney gave the McCoole fight to McCoole that night after Jack Looney and Tom Kehoe promised him $700, paying $300 down

In the Gallagher fight fifty miles from St. Louis ($1,000 a side), Allen was winning when Gallagher's second tossed the sponge as a trick; Gallagher struck Allen as he came to shake hands, Allen jumped the ropes and fled, and the fight was later declared a draw at a meeting on Fourth Street

Allen fought Jem Mace near New Orleans for $2,500 a side, entering the ring at 195 pounds instead of his usual 175 after being seen drunk days before; he claimed a broken arm when thrown and Mace was given the fight
Allen trained for the Mace fight at the Wash Home (town name unreadable) and travelled from St. Louis to New Orleans for it
Allen got half the excursion money from the Mace fight, which he split with his backers Billy Carroll and John Franklin, and played the piano that night with both hands

notes: This conflicts with article 643 on the August 17, 1869 Gallagher fight: 643 gives $500 a side and says Gallagher was well whipped, while this article gives $1,000 a side and a draw. The name of the training place is unclear in the image, so it is not transcribed.
